extracted.intended_audience: Citizens considering ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution; delegates, political leaders, and informed public
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate whether a proposed constitution (here, the U.S. plan) conforms to republican principles and whether it is federal, national, or a mixed government by examining its foundation, sources, operation, extent of powers, and amendment procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive characters of a republican form
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic is (or may be called) a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential: power must be derived from the great body of society, not from a small or favored class. Sufficient: persons administering government are appointed directly or indirectly by the people and hold offices by one of the tenures specified (during pleasure, limited term, or good behavior). Anti-patterns: hereditary nobles or a small oligarchy delegating power yet claiming the republican name; appointment only by legislatures without popular derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete features that satisfy the republican standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare offices and tenures in the proposed constitution to the republican standard: who appoints each branch and what is the tenure?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the plan: House of Representatives elected immediately by the people; Senate appointed indirectly (by States); President indirectly derived from the people's choice; judges to hold by 'good behavior'; specific term lengths (House 2 years, Senate 6 years, President 4 years). Additional republican guarantees: absolute prohibition of titles of nobility and express guaranty of the republican form to each State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation test for federal vs national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine on what assent/ratification the constitution is founded: whether it arises from the people as one aggregate nation or from the people acting as distinct and independent States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal character indicated if ratification is by the several States (each acting as a sovereign body) rather than by a majority of the people of the whole Union. Example guidance: because ratification is by the several States (not by a simple aggregate majority of all citizens), the act establishing the Constitution is described as federal rather than national.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources-of-power test for federal vs national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether ordinary powers are derived from the people in their individual capacity (national) or from the States as political/coequal societies (federal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a branch (e.g., House) derives power immediately from the people it is national in that respect; if another branch (e.g., Senate) derives appointment from States it is federal in that respect. Mixed derivation implies mixed character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operation-of-powers test for federal vs national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the government's powers operate on individual citizens in their personal capacities (national) or operate on the States in their political capacities (federal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If powers usually operate directly on individuals (e.g., ordinary legislative acts, prosecution of private rights), the government leans national; if powers act on States as collective entities (e.g., controversies where States are parties), the government shows federal features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent-of-powers test for federal vs national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the scope of jurisdiction: whether the national legislature has an indefinite supremacy over persons and things or whether its powers are enumerated and residual sovereignty remains with States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A truly national government implies comprehensive supremacy over all persons/things; a federal government leaves residuary and inviolable sovereignty to the States for unenumerated matters. Presence of enumerated powers and retained state sovereignty indicates a federal aspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments/mode-of-change test for federal vs national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the authoritative mode by which future changes/amendments can be introduced (majority of people, majority of States, unanimous States, or a mixed rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ultimate authority to alter resides in a majority of the people the system is national; if it requires concurrence of each State it is federal. A scheme that requires more than a simple majority and computes proportion by States (not citizens), yet permits less than unanimous concurrence, will be mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of the convention: permitted scope of 'alterations and provisions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the commissions/recommendations (Annapolis and Congress) to determine whether a convention was authorized to propose a government 'adequate to the exigencies of the Union' by altering the Articles of Confederation or inserting new provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules of construction: give meaning to each part of the commissions; where parts cannot coincide, the less important gives way to the more important (means sacrificed to the end). Practical implication: power to change titles, insert new articles, and alter old ones is within authorized 'alterations and further provisions', especially when a 'substantial reform' was contemplated.

rubrics_metrics.name: When extraordinary circumstances justify exceeding formal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether considerations of duty, public necessity, and urgency can justify actions by a convention that exceed its strict commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance drawn from practice and precedent: in crisis, 'forms ought to give way to substance'; informal or unauthorized proposals can be legitimate if submitted to 'the people themselves' for final approbation. Factors: evident national exigency, unanimous conviction of delegates, public expectation, and submission of the result to the people's ratification mitigate concerns about exceeded authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions for judging the aggregate power vested in the general government
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating the sum/quantity of power conferred on a general government consider: (1) whether any part of the powers transferred is unnecessary or improper, and (2) whether the entire mass is dangerous to State jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach: reduce powers into constituent classes (see next metric) and for each ask if the power is necessary to the public good; if necessary, adopt it but also guard against perversion or abuse by appropriate restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of powers to organize the review
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the powers conferred on the general government into classes to evaluate their necessity and danger: (1) security against foreign danger; (2) regulation of intercourse with foreign nations; (3) maintenance of harmony and proper intercourse among the States; (4) miscellaneous objects of general utility; (5) restraint of the States from certain injurious acts; (6) provisions for giving due efficacy to all these powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories as a checklist to ensure all public purposes are covered and to balance federal competence against state sovereignty. Examples: powers to declare war, equip fleets/armies, regulate militia, and levy/borrow money fall under 'security against foreign danger.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and scope of security powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether powers tied to national security are necessary and appropriately scoped: declaring war, granting letters of marque, providing armies and fleets, regulating and calling forth the militia, and levying and borrowing money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline: security powers are primitive/essential objects of civil society and should be confided to federal authorities. Question to probe: is it necessary to grant an indefinite power to raise troops and maintain forces in peace as well as in war? Balance necessity of preparedness/self-defense against risks of peacetime standing forces.
